videos.title: How Ulysses S. Grant Broke Lee's Army, and Why No Other Union General Could
videos.desc:
Ulysses S. Grant took command of the Union armies in 1864, and Robert E. Lee, who had beaten every general sent against him, had no answer.**

Seven Union commanders had faced Lee and stepped back after being hit. Grant didn't. This full documentary follows the campaign from the first morning at Shiloh to the surrender at Appomattox, and shows why the Confederacy's best generals feared him more than any other Union commander.

videos.title: What Happened When Grant’s Army Was Ordered to Keep Marching Straight to Richmond
videos.desc:
What happened when Grant’s army was ordered to keep marching straight to Richmond after the Battle of the Wilderness in May 1864.

In the spring of 1864, Ulysses S. Grant broke the Army of the Potomac’s old pattern of fight, bleed, and retreat. After the inferno of the Wilderness, Union columns reached a Virginia crossroads. North meant safety. South meant Robert E. Lee, Spotsylvania Court House, Cold Harbor, and the road to Richmond. Grant turned south—and the Overland Campaign became one continuous, thirty-day meat grinder that locked Lee in place and helped decide the American Civil War.

videos.title: Why James Longstreet Is the Opposite of Every Other Civil War General
videos.desc:
On a sun-drenched afternoon in July 1863, almost every commander in the Army of Northern Virginia believed victory required a glorious charge across an open field. James Longstreet did not. While his peers saw chivalry, he saw a slaughterhouse. This documentary examines why Longstreet was a modern soldier in a 19th-century war: a commander who understood defensive firepower, industrial slaughter, and the death of the Napoleonic charge—then paid for that clarity after Appomattox.

videos.title: The TRUTH Why Robert E. Lee Really Lost the Civil War
videos.desc:
The popular story says Robert E. Lee lost because of Pickett’s Charge and Northern numbers. The real story is darker—and it started long before Gettysburg.

This video examines Lee’s strategic myopia, his refusal to save the Western Theater, a command system that collapsed after Stonewall Jackson’s death, his declining health in 1863, and how Grant turned Lee’s own aggression into a war of attrition the Confederacy could not survive.

This is not Lost Cause mythology. It is the structural, operational, and human reasons the Confederacy failed.

This is the story of how one fragile copper wire became the deadliest weapon of the Overland Campaign — and how close the whole system came to collapsing.

This is the story of the Spencer repeating rifle — the Civil War weapon that shattered the mathematics of battle, broke a century of tactical assumptions, and convinced trained officers that the rules of warfare had been rewritten on the field.

videos.title: What Grant Understood About Richmond That McClellan Refused to Accept Until It Was Too Late
videos.desc:
The strategic insight that ended the Civil War—why Ulysses S. Grant succeeded where George B. McClellan failed.
